analysis.one_liner: Uses federal grants to wipe out Americans' existing medical debt and bans collection and credit reporting of it.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate HELP Committee: introduced May 8, 2024, with two cosponsors, it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Medical Debt Cancellation Act would have directed the Health and Human Services Department to run a competitive grant program paying hospitals to erase the medical debt their patients owe. It would also have gone further: debt collectors and creditors would be barred from collecting any medical debt that existed before the law passed, medical debt would be removed from credit reports, hospitals could not charge interest on past-due bills, and nonprofit hospitals could not bill uninsured patients more than what they generally bill insured patients. Before sending anyone to collections, hospitals would have to check whether the patient qualifies for charity care and tell them about assistance programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of Americans who carry medical debt — a burden that falls hardest on low-income households and people hit by emergency or serious illness. Their debts would be canceled or become uncollectible, their credit reports would be scrubbed of medical debt entries, and they would face no interest charges on past-due hospital bills and clearer notice of charity care and payment assistance before collections start.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a competitive grant program under which HHS pays hospitals to eliminate eligible medical debt owed by their patients, prioritizing safety-net hospitals and debt owed by low-income patients from emergency and non-elective care, and expanding within two years to non-hospital providers [S2].

Amends the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to prohibit any debt collector or creditor from collecting or attempting to collect medical debt incurred before enactment, with a private right of action allowing consumers to sue for compensatory and punitive damages plus attorney's fees [S2].
Amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act to bar credit reporting agencies from including medical debt on consumer reports and requires them to notify consumers when medical debt is removed [S2].

Requires hospitals to screen patients for charity care eligibility at least 45 days before payment is due, bans collecting interest on past-due medical payments, caps what tax-exempt nonprofit hospitals can collect from uninsured patients, and requires any contracted collection agency to follow the same rules [S2].
Requires HHS to publish a public list of federal, state, and local financial assistance programs for medical bills, and to instruct federal health care programs to stop medical debt collections [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, federal taxpayers would fund the grant program to buy out hospital debt (the text sets no dollar amount), hospitals would give up interest income and collections on unpaid and existing medical bills, debt collection firms would lose a large category of business, and credit bureaus would lose medical-debt data they sell.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, debt collectors, credit bureaus, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The grant program has no funding amount in the bill text, so the cost to taxpayers of paying hospitals to cancel debt is unspecified, and a program of this scale could run into the tens of billions [S2].

The retroactive collection ban wipes out debts that hospitals and collection agencies legally held and, in many cases, had purchased; creditors would absorb that loss, and households who strained to pay their medical bills in full would get nothing back [S2].

Hospitals have a real concern that guaranteed cancellation of unpaid bills could encourage aggressive billing up front or require offsetting revenue elsewhere, and the bill's 'supplement, not supplant' rule attempts but cannot fully guarantee against that [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary households, the benefit is direct and large: medical debt is a leading cause of financial hardship and credit damage, and this bill attacks it on every front at once — cancellation, collection, reporting, and billing. The main costs are a large, unspecified federal outlay, losses imposed retroactively on creditors, and no relief for people who already paid. The design targets safety-net hospitals and low-income patients first, which mitigates but does not eliminate the fairness and cost questions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and that is where it died — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on May 8, 2024, joined by Sen. Jeff Merkley; it had two cosponsors, both Democrats [S1, S2, S3].

The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day; the action history records no further steps — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without ever coming to a vote in either chamber [S1, S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, medical debt collection firms, and credit bureaus keep the existing system: no debt is canceled, collections and interest continue, and no federal money is spent on relief. Borrowers with medical debt gain nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals, debt collectors, and credit bureaus

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got to a vote, so no roll calls exist; support was confined to two senators, both Democrats or allied independents, and no Republican cosponsor ever signed on [S3].

industries.note: The bill makes all pre-enactment medical debt uncollectible and requires contracted collection agencies to follow hospital billing protections. Their revenue comes from collecting medical bills from ordinary households, so their interest runs directly against the relief patients would get.

They would be paid through federal grants to cancel patient debt — giving up uncollectible receivables — but they would lose interest income, be barred from overcharging uninsured patients at nonprofits, and face mandatory charity-care screening before collections. Patients get relief either way; hospitals trade collections revenue for grant money.

Medical debt entries would be banned from consumer reports and removed, eliminating a data category the bureaus sell to lenders and others. The cost to consumers of that data — credit damage and worse loan terms — is precisely what the bill removes.

industries.industry: Safety-net hospitals and nonprofit hospital systems
industries.note: They are first in line for the cancellation grants and would be paid for debt they might otherwise write off, though they must agree to cancel recent debt for low-income and emergency-care patients and cannot cut their existing financial assistance. For their low-income patients, their interest in the grants runs alongside patients' interest in relief.
